newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Old crew begins briefing new cosmonauts on Mir.
newsitem.headline: Old crew begins briefing new cosmonauts on Mir.

text.p: The old crew aboard the crippled Mir began a week-long briefing on Friday of the two new Russian cosmonauts who arrived on Thursday night and who will undertake vital repairs later this month, officials said.
The main item on Friday's agenda -- updated emergency evacuation procedures -- highlighted the risks new Mir commander Anatoly Solovyov and engineer Pavel Vinogradov will face in coming months.
"Their first task is to become familiar with evacuation routes, to remind them of instructions in case something happens," said Vsevolod Latyshev, a Mission Control spokesman.

U.S. and Russian officials were discussing the possibility that NASA astronaut Michael Foale would participate in a space walk to inspect a puncture in the Spektr module, which collided with Mir's resupply ship in the worst accident in its history on June 25.

"We've discussed with the Russians the potential of Mike Foale's participating in the EVA on the 3rd of September, but we haven't made any decisions," said NASA spokeswoman Kathleen Maliga. "We're still deciding whether it makes sense or not."

Solovyov, one of the most experienced cosmonauts in the Russian space programme who has performed nine space walks, seems likely to lead the inspection effort. Vinogradov, a first timer in space, has never taken a space walk, called an EVA in space jargon.

"One of the advantages would be that Mike would be returning on the shuttle shortly after that, and so therefore he'd have seen it and could provide the Russians with an extensive debrief," Maliga said.
Foale is scheduled to stay on board until late September when NASA astronaut David Wolf, who is now training outside Moscow, will replace him.

The most pressing repair problem on board Mir is restoring the Elektron oxygen generating system, which has been broken for more than a week. They are now burning oxygen "candles" from their 70-day supply, officials said.

On Thursday deputy flight director Viktor Blagov said the crew would try to bring a power cable into the Kvant-2 module, which is shut off to preserve energy, to start up the older back-up Elektron system.

The crew woke up in the late morning on Friday after the night-time dock-up with the new cosmonauts. They had to dock manually when automatic systems developed a fault 13 metres (yards) from Mir, officials said.

"Soyuz retreated by 25 metres and then docked manually," Flight Director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters on Thursday. "It was a technical malfunction. The situation was not a critical one but we will look into it."

The two Russian cosmonauts on board since February, Vasily Tsibliyev, 43, who had developed heart problems during his mission, and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, are scheduled to return to Earth on August 14.

Before then they will also brief the crew on how the station has changed in recent months and where they have put various supplies. Tsibliyev and Lazutkin will also undergo medical checks and exercises to prepare for their return to Earth.
On August 20 Solovyov and Vinogradov will undertake a risky repair job inside the Mir space station to restore power on Mir, which has run on partial energy since the June accident.
